per_case.answer_text:
Quick steps

1) Join the OpenChat proposals group to view and discuss proposals. (See the FAQ link.)

2) Check eligibility: you can vote with any neuron you own that existed and had a dissolve delay of at least 1 month when the proposal was made.

3) How voting works: you vote to “adopt” or “reject.” Your vote weight is your neurons’ voting power, calculated as stake × dissolve-delay bonus × age bonus. The dissolve-delay bonus ranges linearly from 1 (0 delay) to 2 (1 year). The age bonus ranges from 1 (0 age) to 1.25 (6 months); a neuron must stay undissolving to age and age resets when it starts dissolving. Example: 1,000 CHAT with 1 year dissolve delay and 6 months age = 2,500 voting power.

4) Adoption rules: a proposal is adopted if adopt votes exceed reject votes after 4 days (or a period of quiet) and adopt votes represent at least 3% of total voting power. A vote ends immediately if adopt or reject votes exceed 50% of available voting power. You may still participate during the 4-day period even if the proposal has been resolved so your neuron can earn voting rewards.

5) How to vote from the app: the easiest current method is voting from within OpenChat. If your CHAT neurons are controlled via the NNS dapp (for example from the decentralization sale) you must add your OpenChat User Id as a hot-key for the neuron(s) before voting. To find your OpenChat User Id: open the app, main menu → profile settings → Advanced (bottom).

6) Adding the hot-key (NNS dapp): sign in at the NNS dapp (https://nns.ic0.app/neurons) → My Neuron Staking → Select Nervous System: OpenChat → (if neurons follow your oldest neuron, select that neuron) → Add Hotkey (bottom of neuron page) → paste your OpenChat User Id. If your neurons are configured to follow your oldest neuron you only need to add the hot-key to that one neuron. Remember to add the OpenChat User Id as a hot-key to any new neurons you create.

For more background and a step-by-step guide see the OpenChat governance blog post and the proposals group.

grade.rationale: All steps and rules given (eligibility, voting power formula/bonuses, adoption thresholds and timing, app/NNS hotkey steps, proposals group) are directly supported by the cited FAQ and governance blog sections. The citations are relevant and cover each claim, and answering (not refusing) is appropriate for this question.

per_case.answer_text:
Short answer: not fully end-to-end encrypted yet.

Details: OpenChat runs on the Internet Computer and provides strong platform security, but there is a known risk that a rogue node operator could intercept ingress messages or read memory until SEV‑SNP is available on node machines. Once SEV‑SNP is available the team says users can be extremely confident that, apart from message recipients, their data will not be accessible to others. The team also plans to implement end‑to‑end (e2e) encryption in future so data would be stored encrypted in canister memory (and hence not accessible to rogue node operators regardless of SEV‑SNP), but this will likely be an opt‑in feature for selected chats and may limit some functions (for example search).

grade.rationale: All claims match the security FAQ: current lack of e2e encryption, SEV‑SNP improving confidentiality, rogue node risk, and planned opt‑in e2e with search limitations. However, the answer also cited a storage chunk that is irrelevant to encryption, so citations are not fully appropriate.

Do this from your profile (only available if you’ve selected a non‑English supported language):

1. Enable “translation correction” mode — the toggle appears just below the language selector in your profile. 
2. In the app you’ll see a small translate icon next to each piece of translatable text. Click the icon for the label you want to fix. 
3. A dialog will open showing the language you’re correcting, the original English text and the current translation. Enter your proposed correction and hit Save. 
4. If the text is dynamic it will contain tokens in curly braces ({like so}) — your translation must include the exact same tokens (you may reorder them if needed). 
5. Make sure your suggestion is accurate and fits the UI (keep it concise if space is limited). You can submit and revise suggestions as many times as you like; your saved suggestions will appear in the UI for you until you refresh the page. 
6. The dev team will review your suggestion (they check layout fit and whether the original meaning is preserved). You’ll be notified if it’s approved or rejected; approved corrections may be included in the next release and are rewarded with a tip in CHAT.

Note: you cannot correct the translation of the translation‑correction page itself.

per_case.answer_text: Voting rewards are created by the SNS and accumulated as maturity in neurons that participated in voting. For a given proposal ballot a neuron’s reward is proportional to its voting power relative to the total voting power of the participating neurons for that ballot. Voting power is calculated as: stake × dissolve‑delay bonus × age bonus. The dissolve‑delay bonus runs from 1 (0 delay) up to 2 (1 year delay); the age bonus runs from 1 (0 age) up to 1.25 (6 months age) — for example, 1000 CHAT with a 1 year dissolve delay and 6 months age has voting power 2500. Rewards are generated at an annual rate of 2.5% of total supply, distributed daily (taking into account ballots that ended that day; if no ballots end the rewards carry over). Note that only eligible neurons (must exist and have at least a 1 month dissolve delay at the time the proposal was made) that actually vote earn rewards; if you fail to vote on a proposal you do not earn for that proposal.

grade.rationale: The answer accurately describes how rewards accrue as maturity, proportional to voting power, defines the voting power formula and bonus ranges with the example, states eligibility requirements, daily distribution with carryover, and the 2.5% annual rate. All points are supported by the cited governance chunks.

per_case.answer_text:
The dev team beacon neuron is a small, public neuron the devs configured so anyone can follow it. It follows each dev team member’s neurons and therefore “votes” by proxy when a majority of the dev team votes the same way. The beacon neuron id is 9adf350c7388dfe7277213a5fc8d817c2d5bc6ff6be5870f0d33d9d6dab01fc6. The dev team say they will vote on every proposal, so following the beacon implicitly participates in every vote and can maximise your voting rewards. The beacon’s controller was removed, making it immutable and unable to be changed.  

Should you follow it? That depends on your preference: if you are happy to follow the dev team’s lead and want automatic participation (and the associated rewards), following the beacon is a simple way to do that. If you want to vote yourself on particular topics you can use topic exclusions (for example follow the beacon on the catch‑all but follow your own neuron on specific topics) because you can follow different neurons per topic or follow yourself to exclude a topic. Also, if you have multiple neurons it’s common to set younger neurons to follow your eldest using the catch‑all topic.

grade.rationale: The answer closely matches the cited governance pages: it explains what the beacon neuron is, how it follows dev members and votes by majority, provides the exact neuron ID, notes the controller removal/immutability, and describes following per-topic and exclusions. per_case.answer_text:
Short answer: your report goes to platform moderators for review and they may take action; there are extra rules for suspected child sexual abuse material (CSEA) and you have rights to contest automated sanctions.

What happens next:
- If you reported from a public group, first you can (and should) appeal to the group owners; if you use the message’s context menu to report it, the report is referred to platform moderators for review. (guidelines:6)
- Moderators review the reported content and may take one or more actions: delete the content, freeze the group, delete the group, or suspend the user who posted it. (guidelines:6)
- For suspected CSEA, the system removes the content and suspends the sending account immediately; a human moderator then reviews every such detection. If the moderator finds the automated system wrong, the action is reversed; if confirmed, the material is reported to the National Crime Agency as required by law. (blog:trust_and_safety:5, blog:trust_and_safety:8)
- For other prohibited content, automated classifiers do not result in automatic removal; a high-confidence detection creates a report for human moderators and only a human decision can remove content or suspend an account. (blog:trust_and_safety:5)

Other important points from the terms:
- If an automated system acts against your account, you have the right to contest that decision and obtain a human review; the sanction notice explains how to contest and the option remains available while an account is suspended. If the decision is not upheld, the content and suspension are reversed. (terms:2:safety_moderation_and_reporting.1)
- When CSEA is reported to authorities, a copy is preserved in access‑restricted storage for the period required by law (typically one year), after which it is deleted. (terms:2:safety_moderation_and_reporting.1)
- Reports to authorities include the content and whatever account data the platform holds; the platform’s architecture holds very little personal data (it states it has no names, emails, phone numbers or IP addresses). (blog:trust_and_safety:8, terms:2:safety_moderation_and_reporting.1)
- If you wish to complain about a safety or moderation decision you may use the help channel in the OpenChat Community or email safety@openchatlabs.org; complaints will be acknowledged and investigated. (terms:2:safety_moderation_and_reporting.1)

If you want, tell me whether you reported in a public group or privately and whether you received a sanction notice — I can explain the contest process in more detail.
